intro: Decides who inherits property among Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs when someone dies without a will — and confirms the right to make a will.

sections.p: Since the 2005 amendment, a daughter is a coparcener by birth in a joint Hindu family, with the same rights and liabilities in ancestral property as a son. The Supreme Court held (Vineeta Sharma, 2020) this applies whether or not the father was alive on 9 September 2005.

sections.t: When a man dies without a will
sections.p: His property goes first to Class I heirs, who share equally: mother, widow, sons, daughters, and children of a predeceased son or daughter (and some grandchildren). Only if there are no Class I heirs does it go to Class II heirs (father, siblings and others in order), then to agnates and cognates.
k: Each widow (if more than one) together takes one share
Mother gets a share equal to each child

sections.p: Any property a Hindu woman holds — whether inherited, gifted, bought or received at marriage — is her absolute property, which she can sell, gift or will as she wishes.

sections.t: When a woman dies without a will
sections.p: Her property goes first to her sons, daughters (and children of predeceased children) and husband; then to the husband's heirs; then to her mother and father. Property inherited from her parents goes back to her father's heirs if she has no children; property from her husband or in-laws goes to the husband's heirs.
A Hindu can dispose of any property they own, including their share in coparcenary property, by will. Wills in Tamil Nadu needn't be registered or stamped, but registration helps avoid disputes.
A person who commits or abets the murder of someone is disqualified from inheriting that person's property.
